Mickey Mantle was a switch-hitting outfielder and the Yankees' centerpiece from the nineteen fifties through the early nineteen sixties, combining power from both sides of the plate with blazing speed and graceful defense. His five hundred thirty-six career home runs, World Series heroics, and magnetic personality made him the face of the Yankees' post-DiMaggio era.

Mantle hit five hundred thirty-six home runs, including eighteen in twelve World Series, the most in postseason history; his power from both left and right sides was unmatched. In nineteen fifty-six, he won the Triple Crown, batting three fifty-three with fifty-two home runs and one hundred thirty RBIs—one of only seven players to achieve this feat in the modern era. He was named American League MVP three times in nineteen fifty-six, nineteen fifty-seven, and nineteen sixty-two, and was a twenty-time All-Star.

Mantle played eighteen seasons with the Yankees, winning twelve pennants and seven World Series titles. Nicknamed The Mick, he was beloved for his raw talent and his struggle with injuries that might have made him even greater. He succeeded Joe DiMaggio as the Yankees' superstar and cultural icon, maintaining the franchise's dynasty through the nineteen fifties and sixties. DiMaggio was the predecessor he succeeded as the Yankees' marquee star. Yogi Berra was a contemporary Yankees legend and catcher who caught Mantle's era. Derek Jeter, the future Yankees superstar, would follow a generation later. The Yankees franchise elevated him to legendary status.
